Lessons.Title: Share Sandwiches
ExplanationParagraphs: Lesson goal: represent fair sharing when the number of sandwiches and the number of people do not divide into whole sandwiches. This is the opening exploratory lesson: students may use diagrams and informal language; they are not yet required to write division equations or formally name every fractional amount.

Warm-up: talk about different foods or shapes one could reasonably divide equally and what fairness means for the amount served. Food photographs in the publisher material have independent asset attributions and are not copied here.

Activity 1 — choose, draw and justify: pick two distinct numbers from 2, 3 and 5 as the number of sandwiches and the number of people. Make a drawing or paper cut-out for that sharing story. For example, share two sandwiches equally among three people by cutting each one into thirds and giving everyone two thirds of a sandwich. Other equal-piece decompositions are possible and must be checked for equal *amounts*, not merely piece counts.

Activity 2 — the same amount shown another way: compare two different diagrams representing the same fair sharing situation. A single sandwich may be partitioned in several ways, and each recipient can get pieces that look different while adding up to equal portions. Ask each learner to explain why the amount each person gets is equal and then produce a second valid diagram.

Source alignment: the actual 2021 first-edition public lesson emphasizes learner-selected quantities, equal amounts, alternate representations and peer discussion, not early symbolic quotient mastery. Exact fraction arithmetic can be an extension but must not replace the source's construction and reasoning. Assessment of a learner-drawn model and fairness explanation requires teacher evaluation; the gated original Cool-down and source photographs are not reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equal sharing
KeyConcepts.Definition: Divide a collection of whole objects so each recipient obtains the same total amount.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Equal-sized pieces must be compared using the same whole; recipients need not receive the same-looking pieces.
KeyConcepts.Example: Two sandwiches can be shared among three people so each gets two thirds.

KeyConcepts.Title: Different pieces, equal totals
KeyConcepts.Definition: Fairness concerns the total amount allotted to each person rather than the number of fragments.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Recombine pieces or compare identical-sized models to establish equal amounts.
KeyConcepts.Example: One person gets a half and a sixth, while another gets two thirds of an identical sandwich: both are equal.

KeyConcepts.Title: Exploring sharing before formal division
KeyConcepts.Definition: Students may use words, pictures and physical pieces to explain their thinking.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not insist on a formal fraction equation in this opening lesson; first establish the equal-share model.
KeyConcepts.Example: Three sandwiches shared by two people is one whole and one half for each.

WorkedExamples.Title: Two sandwiches, three friends
WorkedExamples.Question: How can two equally sized sandwiches be divided fairly among three people?
WorkedExamples.Method: Construct two identical area models and partition each into three equal parts.
Steps: Divide each sandwich into three congruent pieces.
Give each person one piece from each sandwich.
Compare the totals: two equal third-sized pieces per person.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Each receives two thirds of a sandwich; a diagram must support the equal amounts.
WorkedExamples.Check: Three shares of two thirds total the original two sandwiches; teacher reviews the drawing.

WorkedExamples.Title: Three sandwiches, two friends
WorkedExamples.Question: How can two friends share three equal-sized sandwiches fairly?
WorkedExamples.Method: Give each friend one whole, then split the third evenly.
Steps: Set aside one whole sandwich for each friend.
Cut the third sandwich into two equal halves.
Give each friend one additional half.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Each friend gets one and one-half sandwiches.
WorkedExamples.Check: Two equal shares of one and one-half reconstruct all three sandwiches.

WorkedExamples.Title: Unequal-looking pieces, equal amount
WorkedExamples.Question: One friend receives one half and one sixth of a sandwich; another receives two thirds. Are the totals equal?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use a common partition into sixths and compare the overall amount.
Steps: Express one half as three sixths.
Add another one sixth to make four sixths.
Express two thirds as four sixths and compare.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Yes. Both receive four sixths or two thirds of a same-sized sandwich.
WorkedExamples.Check: Fairness requires the sandwiches to have the same whole size; two drawings of equal areas can look different.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Same number of pieces means same share
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A large half and a tiny sixth are not the same amount as two equal halves.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Represent each recipient's complete amount as an area fraction of the same-sized sandwich.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Number of people must divide sandwich count evenly
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A remainder in whole sandwiches can be split into equal parts.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Draw fractional pieces and explain why the collection of shares uses all the food fairly.

SummaryPoints: Fair sharing means equal total amounts, even when a person's share is not a whole sandwich.
Multiple drawings and decompositions can be valid for the same sharing story.
The lesson's original open-ended construction and explanations are teacher-reviewed and are not replaced by a numeric family.

Source: Illustrative Mathematics 2021 first edition, Grade 5 Unit 2 Lesson 1, https://im.kendallhunt.com/k5/teachers/grade-5/unit-2/lesson-1/lesson.html; original examples and representations here are Edulytiks-authored.

Lessons.Title: One Piece of One Part
ExplanationParagraphs: Lesson goal: represent and interpret a unit fraction of a unit fraction using diagrams and a single consistent whole. The original 2021 first-edition lesson begins with students' own representations, before formalizing symbolic fraction multiplication in later lessons.

Warm-up (Notice and Wonder): inspect the 2021 source photograph of a pan of macaroni and cheese; students estimate what fraction remains. The picture does NOT show an exact half. Source teacher guidance places the amount between one third and one half (about two fifths); this is a visual estimate, not a measurable equality. Ask students to justify their estimate and identify the full pan as the whole. If the original photograph cannot be displayed under its own image license, use an independently authored, explicitly approximate model rather than presenting the half-full worked-example model as a source photograph.

Activity 1 (Of What?): a pan is half full and Lin eats one third of the remaining macaroni and cheese. The public 2021 Student Facing task asks learners to DRAW their own diagram and explain how it represents the situation. First let students choose and justify a partition; compare different correct orientations. During synthesis, extend partitions through the original full pan to see that one third of one half represents one sixth. Do not require the numerical product or a particular grid orientation as the initial student response.

Activity 2 (The Same, but Different): examine TWO first-party equal-area rectangle diagrams for one fourth of one half. Diagram A partitions a rectangular whole into two vertical halves, then partitions the chosen half into four equal horizontal strips and darkens one. Diagram B partitions the same whole into two horizontal halves, divides the chosen half into four equal vertical strips and darkens one. Ask learners to explain how EACH diagram represents one quarter of one half, then extend the divisions and justify that the dark area is one eighth of the SAME original whole. These are accessible replacement constructions, not copied publisher diagrams A and B.

Source task and assessment boundary: Grade 5 Unit 3 Lesson 1 (2021) asks for self-made drawings, explanation of a third of a half, comparison of two given diagram representations for a quarter of a half, and an argument about the original whole. Teacher review is needed for drawn partitions and equivalent orientations. The original Cool-down is teacher-gated and remains unverified; use the independently authored formative exit task below instead. Student PDF and proprietary image details still need independent evidence.

Original Edulytics formative Cool-down (NOT copied from the teacher-gated 2021 assessment): A garden bed is divided into two equal halves. One half has vegetables. One fourth of that vegetable half is planted with carrots. Draw a rectangle for the WHOLE garden bed, show the partitions and shade the carrot section. What fraction of the WHOLE garden bed is carrots? Explain your drawing. Teacher-scored drawing and explanation; a number alone is insufficient. Teacher rubric is stored separately from this learner-facing prompt.

KeyConcepts.Title: The whole stays fixed
KeyConcepts.Definition: The original complete object is the reference for every fraction of a fraction.
KeyConcepts.Rule: One half of a whole is not a new whole when the final answer is requested as a fraction of the original.
KeyConcepts.Example: One third of a half is one sixth of the full pan.

KeyConcepts.Title: Successive equal partitions
KeyConcepts.Definition: Represent a fraction of an existing equal part by subdividing that part into more equal-sized pieces.
KeyConcepts.Rule: If the whole is halved and a half is divided into three equal pieces, each selected piece is a sixth of the whole.
KeyConcepts.Example: One sixth is shown by one dark part among six equal whole-pan parts.

KeyConcepts.Title: Orientation does not change fraction
KeyConcepts.Definition: Equivalent diagrams may partition in different directions without changing covered area.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare a selected piece with equal areas of the same whole, not merely the shape's orientation.
KeyConcepts.Example: One quarter of one half occupies one eighth of the whole pan.

WorkedExamples.Title: One third of one half
WorkedExamples.Question: A pan is half full. A person eats one third of that half. What fraction of the full pan is eaten?
WorkedExamples.Method: Draw the whole before partitioning the remaining half.
Steps: Split one whole into two equal half-pan areas.
Subdivide the selected half into three equal parts.
Extend the partition across the whole: there are six equal-sized pieces in total.
WorkedExamples.Answer: One sixth of the original full pan.
WorkedExamples.Check: 3 × (1/6) = 1/2 of the whole; teacher reviews whether the diagram actually shows the six equal parts.

WorkedExamples.Title: One fourth of one half
WorkedExamples.Question: Explain why one fourth of one half of the same pan occupies one eighth of the whole.
Steps: Shade half of a 2-by-4 array of eight equal cells.
Select one of the four equal cells within the chosen half.
Count one selected cell among all eight equal whole-pan cells.
WorkedExamples.Answer: One eighth of the whole pan.
WorkedExamples.Check: Four such pieces reconstruct the half; eight reconstruct the whole.

WorkedExamples.Title: Same result, different diagrams
WorkedExamples.Question: A learner partitions a rectangle horizontally, another vertically; both identify one quarter of the same half. Are the areas equal?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare the selected fraction of the original whole, not the orientation.
Steps: In each diagram identify the original whole pan.
Check that each chosen half occupies one of two equal parts.
Check that one quarter of that half is exactly one eighth of the original.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Yes, each dark piece has one eighth of the same total area.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher examines the drawn equal partitions; a matching number alone does not prove visual equivalence.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use the half as a new whole in the final answer
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source asks what fraction of the original full pan is selected.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Extend the partitions to the whole rectangle and recount all equal pieces.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Partition the selected fraction into unequal-sized parts
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A fraction counts equal parts; unequal divisions cannot establish the target value.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Mark equal-length intervals or use a regularly spaced area grid.

SummaryPoints: Fractions of fractions can be made visible by repeatedly partitioning equal parts of the same whole.
One third of a half is one sixth; one fourth of a half is one eighth of the original whole.
Different diagram orientations may show the same amount; a learner must justify why each piece has the claimed area.

Source: Illustrative Mathematics, first edition 2021 Grade 5 Unit 3 Lesson 1, https://im.kendallhunt.com/k5/teachers/grade-5/unit-3/lesson-1/lesson.html; first-party Edulytiks text and area-model examples.

Lessons.Title: Explore the Coordinate Grid
ExplanationParagraphs: Lesson goal: describe the location and size of rectangles precisely enough that a partner can reproduce them. Students experience how adding grid lines and then numbered coordinate axes improves communication. Formal terms coordinate grid, horizontal axis and vertical axis are introduced, while exact coordinate plotting is not an adequate substitute for the partner construction task.

Warm-up: examine an independently authored empty first-quadrant grid whose horizontal and vertical axes run from zero to ten in unit intervals. Describe what the intersecting lines and numbered axes might help a student communicate.

Activity 1 — three-round Draw My Shape: one learner chooses an axis-aligned rectangle and describes it without showing the picture, while a partner reconstructs it. Round 1 uses an ungridded page, round 2 a square unit grid, and round 3 a numbered coordinate grid. Repeat with another rectangle and compare drawings. Observe which directions become unambiguous as grid labels appear.

Activity 2 — Guess Which One: display several rectangles of varying widths, heights and locations in the first quadrant. The partner who does not know the selected rectangle may ask only yes-or-no questions. Include location-specific questions about the horizontal and vertical numbered axes, not only questions about size. For an original example, a rectangle with opposite corners (2, 1) and (6, 4) has width 4 and height 3 and can be distinguished from another 4-by-3 rectangle translated to a different position.

Assessment boundary: drawing, interpreting a partner's description and asking diagnostic questions are teacher-reviewed. An automatically graded question asking only for an isolated coordinate does not establish mastery of describing a full rectangle. The source's three-round card game and original card art are not copied; original Edulytiks rectangle descriptions are provided as accessible substitutes. The publisher's gated Cool-down is not claimed verified.

KeyConcepts.Title: Coordinate grid
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two perpendicular numbered axes and a lattice of intersecting grid lines that describe spatial position.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A complete location description identifies the horizontal and vertical positions, not merely a shape's width.
KeyConcepts.Example: A rectangle may span horizontal coordinates 2 to 6 and vertical coordinates 1 to 4.

KeyConcepts.Title: Horizontal and vertical axes
KeyConcepts.Definition: The horizontal x-axis runs left-right; the vertical y-axis runs up-down from the origin.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Count a horizontal position along x and a vertical position along y; use the correct numbered scale.
KeyConcepts.Example: The point (2, 1) is 2 units across and 1 unit up from the origin.

KeyConcepts.Title: Reconstructing a rectangle
KeyConcepts.Definition: A figure is determined by its location and dimensions relative to the grid.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Name two opposite corners or all four vertices on a specified square-unit grid.
KeyConcepts.Example: Corners (2,1), (6,1), (6,4), (2,4) define a rectangle of width 4, height 3.

WorkedExamples.Title: Describe a grid rectangle
WorkedExamples.Question: How could you tell a partner to draw a rectangle with corners (2,1), (6,1), (6,4), (2,4)?
WorkedExamples.Method: Describe its exact location and side lengths, or supply the four vertices.
Steps: Find the origin and locate the point at x=2, y=1.
Draw a horizontal side four grid units right, then a vertical side three units up.
Complete the rectangle by connecting back to the corresponding vertices.
WorkedExamples.Check: The drawn rectangle is four grid units wide and three high; teacher checks the partner's reconstruction.

WorkedExamples.Title: Same size, different place
WorkedExamples.Question: Are rectangles with opposite corners (2,1)/(6,4) and (3,2)/(7,5) the same location?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare dimensions separately from coordinate position.
Steps: Both x-coordinate differences equal 4 and both y differences equal 3.
Compare the lower-left corners: (2,1) and (3,2).
Conclude that equal size does not imply identical location.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No; they have equal width and height but lie in different grid locations.
WorkedExamples.Check: All four corresponding coordinates of the second rectangle are one unit farther right and up.

WorkedExamples.Title: Ask a discriminating question
WorkedExamples.Question: A guessed rectangle is one of two equal-sized shapes at different coordinates. What question can locate it?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the numbered axes rather than the shape's size alone.
Steps: Observe that both candidate shapes have width 4 and height 3.
Find a property that differs, such as the x-coordinate of the left edge.
Ask whether the left edge lies at horizontal coordinate 2.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The yes/no question distinguishes the rectangle beginning at x=2 from one beginning at x=3.
WorkedExamples.Check: A correct answer requires inspecting the grid's numbered positions, not guessing by visual size.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Identify a rectangle only by its dimensions
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Two equal-sized rectangles may occupy different positions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Include a reference to numbered grid lines, a corner or vertex coordinates.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Switching x and y moves a point and may change the described rectangle.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State the x coordinate first, then the y coordinate; check each against the axis scale.

SummaryPoints: A coordinate grid is useful because gridlines and labeled axes locate figures precisely.
To reconstruct a rectangle, describe both its side lengths and its position on the grid.
Partner drawing, explanation and yes/no question strategies require teacher review beyond any numeric coordinate exercise.
Source: 2021 first-edition Grade 5 Unit 7 Lesson 1, https://im.kendallhunt.com/k5/teachers/grade-5/unit-7/lesson-1/lesson.html; original Edulytiks grid examples and accessible text table.
